blind_spots.blind_spot: A consumer single-board computer as the fielded compute baseline
blind_spots.operator_reality: A US program office buying a thousand nodes needs a controlled BOM: environmental qualification for shock, vibration, and temperature; configuration control so a silent board revision doesn't fracture the fleet; secure boot and anti-tamper because the node sits forward and will be captured; guaranteed lifecycle availability across a five-year sustainment contract; and an OS baseline that can be STIG'd. A Raspberry Pi 5 satisfies none of those, and the redesign to something that does changes thermals, power, and the AI inference budget all at once — which is a re-architecture discovered after the pilot, not during it.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: In the fight they are actually in, the Pi is the correct engineering answer — cheap, available, replaceable, and good enough to survive attrition. The constraint that kills it is a procurement constraint, and they have never been procured by anyone who imposes it.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Distributed AI: Lightweight AI classifiers run on the edge (Raspberry Pi 5), not expensive servers.

blind_spots.blind_spot: C2 integration is asserted generically; no message format, no TAK, no air-defense chain
blind_spots.operator_reality: A counter-UAS detection is only useful if it arrives in the air-defense C2 picture fast enough and in a format that picture accepts — CoT into a TAK server for the SA layer, and a correlated track into the FAAD C2 chain for anything that will cue an effector. 'Can be integrated' is not an interface. And their actual user interface — a browser-based web page per node — is not how an air-defense crew works: on a DoD network that web app needs its own ATO, STIG'd container, and CAC authentication, and at the tactical edge the operator does not have a browser device to spare.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Their Ukrainian users self-integrate — a crew will happily open a web page on a phone because nobody is enforcing an accreditation boundary. That flexibility is exactly what disappears on a US installation.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Can be integrated with situational awareness and C2 systems

blind_spots.blind_spot: A Ukraine-distributed workforce holding RF/ELINT technical data, with no export-control or facility posture described
blind_spots.operator_reality: The moment a US contract vehicle is involved, RF signal-classification technical data becomes export-controlled, and development or storage by non-US persons abroad is a deemed-export problem before it is a contracting problem. Layer on CMMC/NIST 800-171 for handling CUI, a FOCI review for a company whose engineering center is overseas, and the requirement to hold controlled data on a compliant enclave rather than shared drives. This is the gate that stops the transition regardless of how good the sensor is, and it takes quarters to clear — longer than a pre-seed runway.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The Ukrainian engineering team is their genuine competitive advantage and their fastest feedback loop; nothing about the way they have operated so far has priced in that the same structure is a compliance finding on the US side.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Central Office (U.S.): Argus Foresight Inc., Delaware, USA. Representative office in Ukraine: registration in progress

opener_hook: Argus's public pitch deck says Foresight One runs its classifiers on Raspberry Pi 5 and that prototypes are fielded with the 241st Territorial Defense Brigade in Zaporizhzhia and the 34th Marine Brigade in Kherson — the combat validation is real, and it is also the exact bill of materials a US program office cannot put on a sustainment contract.
what_they_do: Builds low-cost passive RF sensor nodes that mesh together to detect, classify, and geolocate small drones for early warning.
